body_markdown:
There’s good news for fans of five cylinders.[As we recently reported](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/audi-five-cylinder-engine-future-plans/) , Audi has confirmed that it will continue to develop its odd-cylinder-count engine for several years to come.


“We’re well aware of the historical meaning of the five-cylinder,” said Audi Sport boss Rolf Michl. ”Evaluations are still running, and people who know me know that I also have a personal relationship to the five-cylinder. It’s so characteristic and also deeply rooted in history,” he said.


The four-ringed firm has been building fivers for 50 years, and long may it continue. Audi isn’t the only carmaker to put the five-pot to good use, however, so let’s take a look at some of the most memorable such motors from Bavaria and beyond.


## Audi


Audi


Audi’s first five was installed in the 100 (above) in 1976. Ingolstadt’s engineers looked at both five- and six-cylinder options for the aerodynamic sedan, but under-hood space and the prospect of the car ending up too nose-heavy meant it was the fiver that got the nod. It came with a 2.1-liter capacity and 134 hp. Diesel versions followed, and then, in 1979, a turbo was bolted on, giving the flagship Audi 200 a boost to 167 hp.


It was with the quattro (top), however, where the five-cylinder motor would leave its indelible mark. Homologated for Group B rallying, in its ultimate form the engine would deliver close to 400 hp and serve up the World Rally Championship title.


Having been fitted to the RS2 and TT, the five-cylinder now only survives in the RS3. With a 2.5 liter capacity, direct injection and turbocharging, it produces 395 hp—almost three times the power in 50 years of development.


## Alfa Romeo


Alfa Romeo


Despite its inherent off-beat and unbalanced nature, the five-cylinder has proven popular in diesel guise. Alfa Romeo’s 2.4-liter JTD is a case in point. Alfa first fitted it to the 156 sedan in 1997, but the gutsy and characterful engine was also deemed sporty enough to be installed in the 159, 166, Brera coupe (above) and Spider. By the end of its life the JTD was pumping out north of 200 hp and those cars were frugal and fast.


## Fiat


Fiat


At stablemate Fiat, the diesel was deployed in the Croma and Marea sedans, but Turin also opted for five cylinders for the two-liter gasoline motor which was most notably used in the Chris Bangle-designed Fiat Coupe of 1993. In normally-aspirated form there was 150 hp available, but by adding a turbo the Coupe become one of the fastest front-wheel drive cars of its day. With 220 in the Turbo Plus edition it was a wild, tire-frying, torque-steery ride, but never failed to put a smile on the driver’s face.


## Ford


Ford


Remember the Premium Auto Group? It brought Jaguar, Land Rover and Volvo under the Blue Oval umbrella and one of the best tech transfers between members was Volvo’s 2.5-liter T5, which Ford put to excellent use in the 2006 Focus ST. Ford took the Swedish five, bolted on a bigger turbo, and added a forged crank and metal-sprayed bores. In the “warm” Focus it made 222 hp, then in the hotter RS it was upped to 300 horses. Finally, in the positively scorching RS500 (above), there was 345 hp on tap.


## GM


Hummer


The 2004 Chevrolet Colorado and GMC Canyon were the first vehicles in the GM stable to get the General’s new 3.5-liter in-line five cylinder. It made around 220 hp, but in such big vehicles it’s fair to say it struggled. It was bored out to 3.7 liters for the Hummer H3 in 2006, but that made precious little difference to the lethargic performance. GM cut its losses and no more fives were forthcoming.


## Honda


Acura


Always keen to experiment, it’s not surprising that Honda had a play around with five-cylinder engines in the late Eighties. Its G-series was offered in two and 2.5-liter versions and, despite driving the front wheels, was mounted longitudinally. In the Honda Vigor (badged Acura for the U.S.) of 1992, the bigger motor made a decent 176 hp. It stuck around in the 1996 TL, gaining electronically adjustable engine mounts to smooth out its slightly lumpy running. The five cylinder quietly made its exit in 1998 and Honda never returned to the idea.


## Land Rover


Land Rover


When BMW bought the Rover Group for a pound, along with the coveted Land Rover brand, the Germans got the benefit of the company’s 2.5-liter five-cylinder turbodiesel TD5 engine. Unlike many under-engineered Rover products, this one was arguably over-engineered, lasting from 1999 to 2007. It was fitted to Discoveries and Defenders, making up to 136 hp and plenty of torque for off-road action.


## Mercedes-Benz


1981 Mercedes-Benz 240D


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Beating Audi to the punch in 1974 was Mercedes-Benz, with the debut of its 240D, which, confusingly, was actually a three liter. It was described by its maker as “the liveliest and fastest diesel in the world.” Frankly that was more of an expression of just how sluggish its rivals were, as the 79-hp 240D still took some 20 seconds to reach 62 mph from rest. New ground was broken in 1978 when Mercedes bolted on a turbo for the 300SD, boosting power to over 120 hp in its final iteration. It was a long-lived lump, powering the G-Wagen, until 1991. Later a 2.7-liter inline-five with 168 hp was deployed in the C, E, G and ML class and shared with DaimlerChrysler bedfellow Jeep for the Grand Cherokee in foreign markets.


## Volvo


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


The T5 has already had an honorable mention thanks to Volvo’s generosity in sharing it with Ford. For its own products, the five-cylinder was first to appear in the Volvo 850 of 1993, delivering 168 hp from its 2.4 liter capacity. A light pressure turbo boosted that to 197 hp, but icon status was only unlocked when it was downsized to 2.3 liters for high-pressure Turbo models, most notably the T-5R and later R which delivered 247 hp. It reached its zenith in the 2004 S60R with 300 horses, and diesels were also offered outside of the U.S. market until they went rather out of fashion in the mid 2010s. Volvo stuck the five in everything it could, from that first 850 to the C30 and C70 coupes, plus the XC60 and XC90 SUVs and S80 sedan.


## VW


Volkswagen


The Volkswagen Group’s VR6 engine certainly earned its keep. It was the basis of the W-12 for Bentley et al, and by lopping a cylinder off, it became the 2.3-liter VR5 of 1997. Fitted in the Golf MkIV, Bora, Passat and New Beetle, it was gutsy engine with its own unique thrum, and its 148 hp was pretty decent in its day. The VR5, in turn, would lead to the Lamborghini V-10 so that’s another reason to celebrate. After its demise in 2005 VW switched to a more conventional inline five of 2.5 liters and, initially the same power output for the Golf/ Beetle, Jetta and Passat. Later that would go up to 170 hp, but in 2003 VW laid it to rest, leaving only Audi in the five-cylinder game.


The post[10 Brands that Embraced the Oddball Five-Cylinder Engine](https://www.hagerty.com/media/lists/celebrating-50-years-of-five-cylinder-fun/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
